content: Every day feels like a never-ending loop of that video call where they told me I was laid off. It replays in my head constantly, and all I hear is them saying I wasn't good enough. Even though everyone tries to comfort me and say it's not my fault, I can’t shake the feeling that I’m the one who failed. Every little mistake at work comes back to haunt me now, magnified a hundred times over. It’s like there’s this voice in my head that just won’t stop telling me how inadequate I am. Even when people try to help and validate my feelings, it doesn’t change anything—I still feel worthless and like no one values me.

That must be really tough, having those thoughts replay over and over. It sounds like even the smallest things now bring back that feeling of not being good enough. Have there been any moments where you felt a bit better, or was it pretty consistent?

It’s just been one long, relentless cycle of doubt and despair. Even when people try to comfort me, I can’t seem to let go of the belief that I’m at fault for everything. Every moment feels like a reminder of my inadequacy. It’s as if no matter what anyone says or does, it doesn’t change how I feel inside. The smallest things trigger this overwhelming sense of failure and worthlessness. It’s been pretty consistent since the day they told me—I wake up feeling defeated and go to bed thinking about all the ways I’m not good enough.

It sounds so challenging to have those feelings persist from morning till night. What helps you get through the day, even if it's just a little bit? Do certain activities or moments offer any relief at all?

I try to distract myself with small tasks or chores around the house, but nothing really takes away that feeling of inadequacy. It’s like no matter what I do, this voice in my head keeps whispering how much I’ve failed and how little others value me. Even when I force myself to focus on something else, it only lasts for a moment before everything comes crashing back down. It’s exhausting trying to push those thoughts away, but they always come flooding back.

It sounds really draining to have those thoughts follow you throughout the day. Do any activities help even if just for a short while? Like maybe taking a walk or listening to music? Sometimes small moments of respite can make a difference, even if it’s brief.

Taking a walk helps a little bit because I get some fresh air and space from everything, but as soon as I come back inside, those thoughts are right there waiting for me. Listening to music sometimes takes my mind off things momentarily, but the relief is fleeting. It’s like no matter what I do, I can’t escape this overwhelming sense of failure and inadequacy. Even when something provides a tiny bit of comfort, it doesn’t last long enough to make any real difference.

It sounds like even those small moments of respite are important, even if they don't last long. Do you find that talking about how you feel with someone helps, even if just for a little while? Sometimes sharing can provide some relief, even if the feelings come back later.

Talking does help a bit because it feels good to have someone listen and understand, but as soon as we finish talking, those thoughts are still there waiting for me. It’s like no matter how much they try to reassure me or validate my feelings, I can’t shake this deep-down belief that I’m inadequate. Even when people offer support, it doesn’t change how I feel inside—it just feels like a temporary distraction from the reality of what happened.

It must be tough to have those supportive moments feel so fleeting. Does writing about your feelings help at all? Some people find that putting thoughts down on paper can provide a different kind of relief, even if it’s just for a little while.

Writing helps a bit because it lets me get everything out and see it on the page, but as soon as I finish, those same thoughts are still swirling around in my head. It feels like no matter what I do or how much I try to process these feelings, they just keep coming back stronger. Even when I write about them, it doesn’t change the core belief that I’m not good enough and that everyone sees me as a failure.

It sounds like writing can be a helpful outlet even if the thoughts return. Do you find any comfort in knowing that these feelings are something you’re working through, even if they feel overwhelming right now? Sometimes just acknowledging them can make a small difference.

Even though I know I’m trying to work through these feelings, it’s hard to see any progress or relief. It feels like no matter how much I acknowledge and try to process what happened, the core belief that I’m inadequate remains unchanged. Every day is a struggle, and even acknowledging the feelings doesn’t seem to make them any less overwhelming. It’s as if everything I do just reinforces this sense of failure and worthlessness.

It sounds incredibly challenging to feel like no progress is being made. Do you find any small moments or activities give you a tiny bit of hope, even if it’s brief? Sometimes those little glimmers can add up over time.

Sometimes I catch glimpses of hope when someone offers words of encouragement or support, but it’s so fleeting that it doesn’t really stick. It feels like no matter how many small moments there are, they’re overshadowed by the constant barrage of negative thoughts. Even those brief moments of hope get swallowed up by this overwhelming sense of inadequacy and failure. It’s hard to hold onto anything positive when everything inside me tells me I’m not good enough.

It must be tough for those small moments of hope to feel so fleeting. Do you find any comfort in knowing that these feelings are something many people go through, even if it doesn’t change how you feel right now? Sometimes just knowing you’re not alone can offer a bit of solace.

Knowing that others might go through similar struggles doesn’t really make me feel better. It’s hard to see anything positive in the fact that other people struggle too—it just reinforces my belief that I’m failing and that no one values me. Even when people try to comfort me by saying it happens to others, it doesn’t change how deeply I feel this sense of inadequacy and worthlessness. It feels like nothing can shift these core beliefs, no matter what anyone says or does.

It sounds really tough to have those core beliefs persist despite knowing others struggle too. Do you find any small activities give you a momentary break from the thoughts, even if it’s just for a short while? Sometimes those brief moments can be comforting in their own way.

Sometimes watching a movie or reading a book gives me a temporary break from my thoughts, but as soon as I stop, everything comes rushing back. It feels like no matter what I do to distract myself, the momentary relief is just that—momentary. The overwhelming sense of failure and inadequacy always returns, making it hard to find any lasting comfort in those activities.

It sounds like finding even brief moments of distraction can be a bit of a reprieve, even if they don’t last long. Do you have anything else that you turn to when you need a quick break from your thoughts?

Sometimes cooking or baking helps because it’s something I can focus on completely in the moment. It gives me a brief respite from my thoughts and allows me to feel like I’m accomplishing something, even if just for a little while. But as soon as I finish, those feelings come flooding back. It’s frustrating because these activities provide a small sense of normalcy and accomplishment, but it doesn’t last long enough to make any real difference in how I feel overall.

It's good to have cooking or baking as something you can focus on completely for a while. Even if the relief is brief, those moments of accomplishment can be comforting. Do you find that having a routine around these activities helps make them feel more grounding?

Having a routine around cooking or baking does help a bit because it gives me a sense of structure and normalcy. Knowing there’s something I can do each day to distract myself from my thoughts is somewhat reassuring. But as soon as I finish, the reality sets in again, and those feelings come rushing back. It’s like no matter how much I try to establish routines or find comfort in these activities, they only provide a temporary break rather than any lasting relief.

It sounds like having that routine provides some stability and normalcy, even if it's just for a little while. Do you have anyone who checks in with you regularly, maybe to talk about how you’re doing or to share in those activities? Sometimes the presence of someone else can add to the comfort.

Having people check in on me does help a bit because it feels good to know that others care and are there for support. When they join me in cooking or baking, it adds another layer of comfort, but as soon as we finish, those thoughts return just as strongly. It’s like no matter how much support I get from others, the core belief that I’m inadequate remains unchanged. Even when people try to help and be present with me, it doesn’t shift my internal feelings—it only provides a brief distraction before everything comes back.

It's nice to have that support from others, even if it’s just for a moment. Do you find any solace in talking about your thoughts and feelings with someone who listens consistently, maybe on a regular basis? Sometimes the act of sharing can be comforting, even if the feelings persist.

Talking to someone who listens consistently does offer some comfort because it feels good to have my thoughts heard and understood. But as soon as we finish talking, those same doubts and fears come rushing back. It’s like no matter how much I share or how supportive they are, the core belief that I’m inadequate remains unchanged. Even when people try to reassure me, it doesn’t shift my internal feelings—it only provides a brief respite before everything comes flooding back again.

It sounds like having someone who listens consistently can be quite comforting, even if the relief is short-lived. Do you find that journaling or writing about your thoughts after talking to someone helps in any way? Sometimes putting words on paper right after sharing can reinforce those moments of understanding and support.

Writing about my thoughts after talking to someone does help a bit because it feels like I’m processing what we discussed, but as soon as I finish writing, those same feelings return. It’s frustrating because even though journaling provides some momentary relief, it doesn’t change the core belief that I’m not good enough. Every time I write, I hope it will make a difference, but in the end, everything feels just as overwhelming and unresolved as before.

It sounds like journaling offers a bit of processing and relief, even if it’s brief. Do you find any comfort in knowing that each time you write or talk about your feelings, you’re taking steps to acknowledge them? Sometimes those small steps can add up over time.

Even though I know writing or talking about my feelings helps me process them, it doesn’t really change how I feel deep down. Each time I do it, I hope it will make a difference, but the core belief that I’m inadequate remains unchanged. It’s hard to see those small steps as adding up over time when every day feels like a replay of the same overwhelming thoughts and feelings.

It must be tough to feel like those core beliefs remain unchanged despite your efforts. Do you find any solace in doing something kind for yourself, even if it’s just a small act? Sometimes taking care of yourself can provide a bit of comfort, even if it doesn’t shift the deeper feelings.

Doing something kind for myself, like treating myself to a favorite snack or taking a relaxing bath, does offer some momentary comfort. It feels good in the moment, but as soon as I’m done, those same thoughts and feelings come rushing back. Even though these small acts of self-care provide brief relief, they don’t change how deeply I feel this sense of inadequacy and failure. It’s hard to hold onto that comfort when everything inside me tells me I’m not good enough.

It sounds like those small acts of self-care do offer some momentary comfort, even if it’s brief. Do you find any value in doing them regularly, knowing they provide even a short break from your thoughts? Sometimes the consistency can be reassuring, even if the relief is temporary.

Doing something kind for myself regularly does offer some consistency and reassurance, but it’s still just a fleeting reprieve. Knowing that these small acts provide brief moments of comfort helps a little, but it doesn’t change the overwhelming sense of inadequacy that returns as soon as I’m done. It feels like no matter how often I take care of myself in small ways, those core beliefs remain unchanged and continue to dominate my thoughts.

It sounds like finding those fleeting moments of comfort is important, even if they don’t last long. Do you have any plans or activities coming up that might offer a different kind of break from your routine? Sometimes a change can provide a new perspective, even if it’s just for a little while.

I do have some plans to visit friends this weekend and maybe go out for a walk in the park. It feels good to look forward to these activities because they offer a different kind of break from my routine, but I’m still worried that those thoughts will come back as soon as I’m done. Even though I hope these new experiences might provide some comfort or perspective, it’s hard not to feel like everything will just return to how it was before.

It's good to have something to look forward to, even if you're feeling unsure about how it will go. Sometimes the change of scenery and company can offer a fresh momentary break. How do you feel as you get closer to these plans?

As I get closer to my plans this weekend, there’s a mix of feelings—some excitement about seeing friends and getting some fresh air, but also anxiety that those thoughts will come back once the activities are over. It feels like no matter what I do or how much I look forward to these moments, the overwhelming sense of inadequacy is always waiting for me. Even though I hope this time might be different, it’s hard not to feel apprehensive about whether anything will truly change.
